title: Useful concepts
html:
You will meet these concepts in the GiveWell model, the quiz and the workbook.

Theory of change

A theory of change spells out how an intervention is supposed to work: what you will do, why that should lead to impact, and what you are assuming.

Malaria Consortium’s theory of change for seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC): “If we distribute preventive antimalarial drugs to children during peak transmission season, and if caregivers administer them correctly, then fewer children will contract malaria, leading to fewer deaths.”

Each “if” is an assumption that could fail. Children might not take the medicine. The drugs might be counterfeit. Writing the assumptions down means they can be tested.

The evidence hierarchy

Some evidence is more trustworthy than other evidence:

  • Strongest: systematic reviews combining several rigorous studies; large, well-run randomised controlled trials (RCTs), especially ones replicated in different settings.

  • Moderate: individual RCTs; quasi-experimental designs (natural experiments, before-and-after with comparison groups); well-designed observational studies.

  • Weaker: before-and-after comparisons without control groups; correlational studies; case studies.

  • Weakest: theory and plausibility alone; testimonials and cherry-picked success stories.

When you assess a claim about impact, ask where its evidence sits.

Why RCTs matter

Suppose people who took a job training programme earn more afterwards. Did the programme cause that, or would they have found better jobs anyway? An RCT answers this by assigning people at random to receive the programme or not. The two groups are then alike in every way except the programme, so a difference in outcomes can be attributed to it.

RCTs aren’t always possible, and they don’t tell you whether an intervention is the best use of money. Where RCT evidence exists, weigh it heavily.

What outcomes might we measure?

QALYs (quality-adjusted life years) count years of life, adjusted for health. One QALY is one year in full health. A year with a condition that reduces quality of life by 30% counts as 0.7. The UK’s NHS typically funds treatments costing less than £20,000–30,000 per QALY gained.

DALYs (disability-adjusted life years) count years of healthy life lost, so they are the mirror image of QALYs. You met them in Ord’s essay last week. The WHO uses them to compare the burden of different diseases. GiveWell uses its own moral weights instead (see the moral weights lesson), with the same aim: one common unit for different outcomes.

WELLBYs (wellbeing-adjusted life years) measure how satisfied people say they are with their lives. One WELLBY is a one-point change on a 0–10 life satisfaction scale for one person for one year. This allows comparison of interventions that affect wellbeing but not health, such as treating depression or reducing loneliness.

None of these measures is neutral. QALYs and DALYs assume a disability lowers wellbeing by a fixed amount, yet people with disabilities often report higher wellbeing than the weights imply. WELLBYs assume that self-reports are valid and comparable between people.
